subject: GCSE Science
source: Drive: Science Overview sequence and AQA GCSE 9-1 required practical handbooks (8461/8462/8463/8464) adapted; AQA 8464 Combined Science Trilogy specification

lessons.title: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells
objectives: Describe the function of the main sub-cellular structures in animal, plant and bacterial cells
Compare eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells
Explain why plant cells have extra structures that animal cells lack

keywords.def: an organism whose cells have a nucleus enclosed by a membrane
a single-celled organism whose cells have no nucleus; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm
structures where aerobic respiration releases energy
tiny structure where proteins are made
a small extra ring of DNA found in bacterial cells

starter: Bismillah. What is the basic building block of all living things?
Name two structures found in a plant cell that are not found in an animal cell (KS3).
What piece of equipment do we use to look at cells, and what does it do?

teach.heading: Two types of cell
bullets: Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus: animals, plants, fungi and protists.
Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus: bacteria are prokaryotes.
Prokaryotic cells are much smaller, often about 1 µm across.
Eukaryotic cells are typically 10 to 100 µm across.
teach.note: Start by asking pupils to predict which of a human cheek cell, an onion cell and E. coli has no nucleus. Link to Qur'an 51:21 ('and in yourselves - will you not see?') as an invitation to look closely at how we are made. Misconception: bacteria DO have DNA; it simply is not inside a nucleus.

teach.heading: Animal cell structures
bullets: Nucleus: contains DNA and controls the cell's activities.
Cytoplasm: gel where most chemical reactions happen.
Cell membrane: controls which substances enter and leave.
Mitochondria: site of aerobic respiration, releasing energy.
Ribosomes: where proteins are made (protein synthesis).
teach.note: Use a labelled diagram on screen and ask pupils to give function in one short phrase. Stress that exam answers need the function, not just the name. Common error: saying mitochondria 'make energy' - energy cannot be made, it is transferred or released from glucose during respiration.

teach.heading: Extra structures in plant cells
bullets: Cell wall made of cellulose: strengthens and supports the cell.
Permanent vacuole: filled with cell sap, keeps the cell firm.
Chloroplasts: contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis.
Only cells exposed to light have chloroplasts, not root cells.
teach.note: Ask: why would a root cell not need chloroplasts? (No light underground, so no photosynthesis.) This is a typical 'explain' application question. Remind pupils that the cell wall is different from the membrane: the wall is rigid and fully permeable, the membrane is selective.

teach.heading: Bacterial cells
bullets: Cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes are present.
Genetic material is a single DNA loop, not in a nucleus.
Plasmids: small rings of extra DNA, useful in genetic engineering.
Some bacteria have a flagellum to move.
teach.note: Highlight that the bacterial cell wall is not made of cellulose (it is a different material). Ask pupils to say two ways a bacterium is similar to and two ways different from an animal cell. Introduce the word 'whereas' for comparison answers.

teach.heading: Comparing cells in the exam
bullets: Command word 'compare' needs a similarity or difference for BOTH cells.
Use comparative words: whereas, both, larger, smaller, unlike.
Eukaryote: DNA in a nucleus. Prokaryote: DNA in a loop.
Always link a structure to its function for full marks.
teach.note: Model a 4-mark 'compare' answer live: 'Both cells have a cell membrane and ribosomes, whereas only the plant cell has chloroplasts for photosynthesis.' Show how one sentence earns the mark by naming both sides.

practice: Match each structure to its function: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosome, cell membrane, chloroplast.
A student says 'a bacterium has no DNA because it has no nucleus'. Explain what is wrong with this.
Name three structures found in both a plant cell and a bacterial cell.
independent: Draw and label an animal cell, a plant cell and a bacterial cell, adding a one-line function for each label.
Compare a prokaryotic cell with a eukaryotic cell. (4 marks)
A palisade cell has many chloroplasts but a root hair cell has none. Explain why. (2 marks)
exit: Which part of an animal cell releases energy from glucose?
State one difference between where the DNA is found in a bacterial cell and in a plant cell.
lessons.homework: Make a one-page comparison table of animal, plant and bacterial cells with functions, and learn it for a quick test next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: give a pre-labelled diagram plus a word bank with symbols; sentence starters for 'compare' answers. Stretch: explain why a larger eukaryotic cell needs mitochondria in greater number than a bacterium.

lessons.title: Microscopy and magnification calculations
objectives: Compare light and electron microscopes in terms of magnification and resolution
Calculate magnification, image size and real size using units correctly
Describe the required practical: preparing and observing a slide of plant cells

keywords.def: how many times larger an image is than the real object
the ability to distinguish two close points as separate
one millionth of a metre; 1 mm = 1000 µm
a microscope that uses electrons, giving higher magnification and resolution than a light microscope

starter: Name three structures found in both plant and animal cells.
Convert 2.5 cm to millimetres.
Explain why bacterial cells are classed as prokaryotes.

teach.heading: Light and electron microscopes
bullets: Light microscope: cheap, portable, can view living cells in colour.
Electron microscope: much higher magnification and resolution.
Electron microscopes show ribosomes and the detail inside mitochondria.
Better resolution means finer detail can be seen.
teach.note: Explain that magnification makes the image bigger but resolution decides whether the extra size shows more detail. Use the analogy of enlarging a blurry photo: it gets bigger but not clearer. Mention that Ibn al-Haytham's work on light and lenses in the 11th century helped lay foundations for optics, which later made microscopes possible.

teach.heading: The magnification triangle
bullets: magnification = image size ÷ real size.
Measure the image with a ruler, in millimetres.
Convert to the same units before calculating.
teach.note: Draw the formula triangle I over (M x R). Worked example 1: a cell image measures 45 mm and the real cell is 0.15 mm, so magnification = 45 ÷ 0.15 = ×300. Ask pupils which units must match.

teach.heading: Worked examples with units
bullets: Image 12 mm, magnification ×400: real size = 12 ÷ 400 = 0.03 mm.
Standard form: 0.03 mm = 3 × 10⁻² mm.
Show every step: formula, substitution, answer with unit.
teach.note: Work example 2 on screen, then ask pupils to try: image 60 mm, real size 0.2 mm (answer ×300). Common error is mixing mm and µm; insist on converting first. Exam tip: 'calculate' questions give marks for method even if the final answer is wrong.

teach.heading: Required practical: observing cells
bullets: Place a thin onion epidermis on a slide with a drop of water.
Add iodine, lower the coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles.
Start on the lowest power objective and focus with the coarse knob.
Draw with a sharp pencil, no shading, clear lines, label, add magnification.
teach.note: SAFETY AND ONLINE DELIVERY: teacher demonstrates live via a camera on the microscope, or show a school-approved video of slide preparation. Iodine stains skin and clothes and the scalpel is sharp, so pupils at home should not cut onion or handle scalpels; instead give each pupil a printed or on-screen micrograph with a scale bar for the drawing task and calculation. A virtual microscope simulation is an acceptable alternative.

teach.heading: Drawing and exam rules
bullets: Draw large, use a pencil, continuous lines, label lines straight.
Show the scale bar or write the magnification.
Label only what you can see, do not guess.
Command word 'calculate' needs a unit.
teach.note: Show a good and a poor scientific drawing side by side and let pupils spot five differences. Link to amanah and truthfulness: scientists record what they actually observe, not what they expect.

practice: An image of a plant cell is 36 mm wide. The real cell is 0.12 mm. Calculate the magnification.
A ×500 micrograph shows a mitochondrion 4 mm long. Calculate its real length in µm.
Give two advantages of electron microscopes over light microscopes.
independent: A micrograph of a sperm cell has a scale bar of 20 mm representing 10 µm. Find the magnification and the real length of a sperm head that measures 35 mm on the image.
Write a method for preparing a slide of onion cells with the correct order of steps and one safety point.
Explain why electron microscopes allowed scientists to discover the internal structure of mitochondria. (3 marks)
exit: Write the equation linking magnification, image size and real size.
Convert 0.045 mm into µm.
lessons.homework: Complete five magnification calculations on a worksheet, converting units each time, and label a micrograph supplied by your teacher.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a magnification calculation template with boxes for each step. EAL: key terms with images. Stretch: convert answers into standard form and calculate the actual size of a bacterium from a scale bar.

lessons.title: Specialised cells, differentiation and stem cells
objectives: Explain how structure relates to function in specialised cells
Describe differentiation in animals and plants
Discuss the uses, benefits and risks of stem cells

keywords.def: the process by which a cell becomes specialised for its job
a cell with a structure adapted to carry out a particular function
an undifferentiated cell that can divide and develop into other cell types
plant tissue where stem cells are found, at the tips of roots and shoots

starter: What is the function of a mitochondrion?
Calculate magnification if the image is 24 mm and the real size is 0.08 mm.
Why do root cells not contain chloroplasts?

teach.heading: Specialised animal cells
bullets: Sperm: tail to swim, many mitochondria, acrosome with enzymes.
Nerve cell: long axon and branched dendrites to carry impulses.
Muscle cell: protein fibres that contract; many mitochondria.
Structure is always linked to function.
teach.note: Pick a cell and ask pupils to 'say it as a chain': feature, what it does, so it helps with the function. For example, 'sperm have many mitochondria, to release energy from respiration, so the tail can swim to the egg.' Misconception: cells do not choose to become specialised; their genes are switched on or off.

teach.heading: Specialised plant cells
bullets: Root hair cell: long extension gives large surface area for absorption.
Xylem: hollow, strong with lignin; transports water and minerals.
Phloem: sieve plates and companion cells transport sugars.
teach.note: Show a root hair diagram. Ask: why is a large surface area helpful for absorbing water by osmosis and minerals by active transport? Link to next lessons. Mention Qur'an 21:30 which says that Allah made every living thing from water; plant cells show how central water is.

teach.heading: Differentiation
bullets: Differentiation: cells change to become specialised.
Most animal cells differentiate early and then cannot change.
Many plant cells can differentiate throughout life.
Specialised cells divide by mitosis only to make more of the same type.
teach.note: Use the analogy of a school: all pupils start in Reception with the same potential and then follow different courses. Check pupils understand that every cell has the same genes; differences come from which genes are active.

teach.heading: Stem cells and their uses
bullets: Embryonic stem cells can become any type of human cell.
Adult stem cells, e.g. in bone marrow, form only some cell types.
Meristems in plants can produce any plant cell type, for life.
Uses: replace damaged cells, e.g. in diabetes and paralysis.
teach.note: Explain therapeutic cloning: an embryo with the same genes as the patient is made, so the stem cells would not be rejected. Plant meristems are used to clone rare plants quickly and to grow disease-resistant crops.

teach.heading: Risks and ethical issues
bullets: Risk: stem cells grown in a lab may carry viruses.
Some people object to using embryos, as potential human life.
Others support it because it can treat serious disease.
Evaluate arguments using evidence, not just opinion.
teach.note: Run a respectful discussion. Explain that religious scholars, including Muslim scholars, have debated this question at length and that views differ; the goal is to practise presenting reasoned arguments for and against. In the exam: give both sides, then a balanced conclusion.

practice: Explain how the structure of a nerve cell helps it to carry electrical impulses.
State two differences between differentiation in animals and in plants.
Suggest why bone marrow stem cells cannot be used to grow a whole new heart.
independent: Create a table of four specialised cells with: adaptation, how it helps, function.
Describe how stem cells from bone marrow could be used to treat a patient. (3 marks)
Evaluate the use of embryonic stem cells in medicine. (4 marks)
exit: Define the term 'differentiation'.
Give one risk of using stem cells in treatment.
lessons.homework: Write a six-line explanation of why root hair cells and sperm cells have different structures even though they have the same genes.
lessons.send: SEND: use diagram cards with features to match to functions. EAL: give frame 'The ... has ... so that it can ...'. Stretch: explain how meristem cells are used in plant cloning and why this matters for growing crops.

lessons.title: The cell cycle and mitosis
objectives: Describe the stages of the cell cycle including DNA replication and mitosis
Explain why mitosis is important for growth, repair and asexual reproduction
Describe cancer as uncontrolled cell division

keywords.def: a thread-like structure of DNA in the nucleus carrying genes
cell division that produces two genetically identical daughter cells
the series of stages a cell goes through from one division to the next
a mass of abnormal cells caused by uncontrolled division

starter: Where in a cell is the DNA found in a eukaryote?
Name two types of stem cell.
State the difference between a specialised and an unspecialised cell.

teach.heading: Chromosomes and genes
bullets: DNA is coiled into chromosomes in the nucleus.
Human body cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in total).
A gene is a short section of DNA coding for a protein.
One chromosome in each pair is from each parent.
teach.note: Show a human karyotype image. Check the difference between a chromosome, a gene and DNA with a quick whiteboard poll. Point out that pairs mean 23 pairs, which gives 46 chromosomes; pupils often write 23 for the number in a body cell.

teach.heading: The cell cycle
bullets: Stage 1: cell grows, makes more ribosomes and mitochondria.
Stage 2: DNA replicates so there are two copies of each chromosome.
Stage 3: mitosis, chromosomes pulled apart to opposite ends.
Stage 4: cytoplasm and membrane divide to form two cells.
teach.note: Draw a circular cycle diagram. Ask: why must the cell grow and copy its DNA before dividing? Because each daughter cell needs a full set of genetic material and enough organelles. Names of mitosis phases (prophase etc.) are not required for GCSE Combined Science.

teach.heading: Mitosis step by step
bullets: The nucleus membrane breaks down.
Chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell.
Copies are pulled to opposite poles, then two nuclei form.
Result: two genetically identical diploid cells.
teach.note: Use a short video or animated model to show chromosomes moving. Use a 'think-pair-share' question: 'Why is it important that the daughter cells are identical?' Answer: because they must carry out the same job as the parent cell.

teach.heading: Why mitosis matters
bullets: Growth of multicellular organisms by increasing cell number.
Repair of damaged tissue, such as skin after a cut.
Asexual reproduction, e.g. strawberry runners and Hydra budding.
teach.note: Give pupils a context question: skin cells divide about every two weeks, nerve cells hardly divide at all. Ask why a cut on the finger heals but spinal nerve damage rarely does. Link to differentiation from lesson 3.

teach.heading: Uncontrolled division: cancer
bullets: Cancer: changes in cells cause uncontrolled division, forming a tumour.
Benign tumours stay in one place and do not invade.
Malignant tumours invade neighbouring tissue and spread by the blood.
Risk factors: smoking, UV radiation, some genes, some viruses.
teach.note: Be sensitive: some pupils may have family experience of cancer. Focus on science and prevention. Mention that Muslims are encouraged to take care of their health and to seek treatment. Exam link: 'benign' versus 'malignant' is a typical 2-mark question.

practice: Put these in order: DNA replicates; cell membrane divides; cell grows; chromosomes pulled apart.
A human skin cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will each daughter cell have after mitosis?
Explain why DNA must replicate before mitosis.
independent: Draw a flow chart of the cell cycle with one sentence for each stage.
Explain two reasons why mitosis is needed in a growing tree. (2 marks)
Compare a benign tumour with a malignant tumour. (3 marks)
exit: What is the name of the type of cell division that produces identical cells?
State one risk factor for cancer.
lessons.homework: Create a labelled diagram of mitosis with captions showing how 2 chromosomes become 2 identical cells.
lessons.send: SEND: use a pre-printed sequence cards activity. EAL: key term cards with pictures. Stretch: calculate the number of cells after 5 divisions (2^5) and discuss why a tumour grows quickly.

lessons.title: Diffusion, surface area and active transport
objectives: Define diffusion and describe factors that affect its rate
Calculate surface area to volume ratios and explain why they matter
Compare diffusion with active transport

keywords.def: the net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration down a concentration gradient
a difference in concentration between two regions
movement of substances from a lower to a higher concentration using energy from respiration
how much surface an object has compared with its volume

starter: What does the cell membrane do?
Name two substances that cells need to take in.
Why do cells need energy from respiration?

teach.heading: What is diffusion?
bullets: Net movement of particles from high to low concentration.
Passive: it needs no energy from the cell.
Examples: oxygen into cells, carbon dioxide out, urea into blood.
Particles move randomly, but more move down the gradient.
teach.note: Demonstrate with a drop of food colouring in warm and cold water (video or teacher camera). Misconception: particles do not 'know' where to go; random movement produces a net movement. Always say 'net movement' in exam answers.

teach.heading: Factors that affect diffusion rate
bullets: Bigger concentration difference: faster diffusion.
Higher temperature: particles move faster, so faster diffusion.
Larger surface area: more particles can cross each second.
teach.note: Ask pupils to predict the effect of each factor then justify. Encourage use of a 'because' chain. Exam tip: if asked 'explain how temperature affects diffusion', mention particles have more kinetic energy.

teach.heading: Surface area to volume ratio
bullets: 1 cm cube: surface area 6 cm², volume 1 cm³, ratio 6:1.
2 cm cube: surface area 24 cm², volume 8 cm³, ratio 3:1.
Larger organisms have a smaller ratio, so need exchange systems.
Single-celled organisms exchange across their surface.
teach.note: Work through the cube calculation slowly: surface area = 6 x side squared. Many pupils forget to multiply by 6 faces. Ask: why can an amoeba rely on diffusion but a human cannot? The ratio is too small for a human body, so lungs, villi and a circulatory system are needed.

teach.heading: Adaptations of exchange surfaces
bullets: Alveoli: thin walls, moist, rich blood supply, large surface area.
Villi in small intestine: large surface area, thin wall, blood capillaries.
Root hair cells: long extension increases surface area for absorption.
Short diffusion distance and steep gradient maintained by blood flow.
teach.note: Stress that you need to link adaptation to effect on diffusion: thin wall means short diffusion distance; rich blood supply keeps the concentration gradient steep. Qur'an 3:190-191 invites reflection on creation; the lungs are a striking example of efficient design in living things.

teach.heading: Active transport
bullets: Moves substances from low to high concentration, against the gradient.
Needs energy from respiration.
Root hair cells take in mineral ions such as nitrate.
Gut absorbs glucose into the blood by active transport.
teach.note: Use a bike analogy: diffusion is going downhill, active transport is going uphill and needs pedalling. Ask pupils to say why root cells have many mitochondria (to supply energy for active transport).

practice: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a 3 cm cube.
State two ways the small intestine is adapted for absorption.
Explain why a goldfish can survive using diffusion across its gills but an elephant needs a lung and blood system.
independent: Copy and complete a table comparing diffusion and active transport using: direction, energy needed, example.
Explain how a root hair cell is adapted to take up water and mineral ions. (4 marks)
A student claims that a higher temperature slows diffusion. Evaluate this claim using ideas about particles. (3 marks)
exit: Define diffusion using the term 'concentration gradient'.
Why do cells that carry out active transport contain many mitochondria?
lessons.homework: Calculate the surface area to volume ratios of cubes with sides 1 to 5 cm and plot a graph; write a sentence describing the trend.
lessons.send: SEND: use block models or digital manipulatives to see the cubes. EAL: pre-teach 'net', 'gradient', 'against'. Stretch: explain why a flattened worm can exchange gases without lungs.

lessons.title: Osmosis and the required practical
objectives: Define osmosis and predict the direction of water movement
Describe the effect of osmosis on plant and animal cells
Process and interpret data from the potato cylinder required practical

keywords.def: the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
a membrane that lets some substances through but not others
firm and swollen because a plant cell is full of water
a plant cell whose membrane has pulled away from the cell wall after losing water

starter: Define diffusion in one sentence.
Why does active transport need energy?
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a 4 cm cube.

teach.heading: What is osmosis?
bullets: Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a partially permeable membrane.
Water moves from dilute solution to concentrated solution.
Think: water moves from high to low water concentration.
Solute particles are too big to cross the membrane.
teach.note: Draw a membrane with small water molecules and large sugar molecules. Remind pupils that 'dilute' means lots of water. Misconception: 'water moves towards salt' is shorthand but incomplete; use the proper explanation with concentration of water.

teach.heading: Osmosis in cells
bullets: Plant cell in pure water: gains water, becomes turgid.
Plant cell in strong sugar solution: loses water, becomes flaccid then plasmolysed.
Animal cell in pure water: may burst.
Animal cell in strong solution: shrivels.
teach.note: Use cartoon diagrams with arrows. Ask why turgid plant cells are helpful (they support the plant and make leaves firm; wilting happens when cells lose water). Explain that animal cells lack a cell wall so cannot resist bursting.

teach.heading: Required practical: potato cylinders
bullets: Cut identical cylinders of potato, same length and diameter.
Weigh each and place in different sugar concentrations for 30 minutes.
Blot dry and re-weigh each cylinder.
Control variables: volume of solution, temperature, time, potato type.
teach.note: SAFETY AND ONLINE DELIVERY: the cork borer and knife are sharp, so this is a teacher demonstration on camera or a school-approved video. Pupils at home may do a kitchen version only with adult supervision: pre-cut chips of equal size, salt in water at different strengths, a kitchen scale (to 0.1 g). Otherwise supply the results table below for analysis. Ask: what is the independent variable? (concentration). What is the dependent variable? (change in mass).

teach.heading: Processing the results
bullets: % change = (final − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100.
Example: 2.50 g to 2.75 g is +10 %.
Example: 3.00 g to 2.55 g is −15 %.
Where the graph line crosses zero, concentrations are equal.
teach.note: Work both examples. Emphasise that negative means water lost. Show a graph with the line crossing zero at about 0.35 mol/dm³: the cell contents and the solution have the same concentration, so no net water movement. Exam tip: use the zero crossing to estimate the concentration inside the potato cells.

teach.heading: Evaluating the experiment
bullets: Repeat and calculate a mean to reduce random error.
Use percentage change so cylinders of different mass can be compared.
Dry each cylinder in the same way before weighing.
Use more concentrations for a more precise result.
teach.note: Ask pupils to suggest one limitation of the method and one improvement. Link to the Islamic ideal of careful and honest recording. Check understanding of 'precision', 'repeatable' and 'valid' because these vocabulary words are often tested.

practice: A potato cylinder has an initial mass of 4.00 g and a final mass of 4.36 g. Calculate the percentage change.
Explain why a plant cell in distilled water does not burst.
Name three variables that should be controlled in the potato cylinder practical.
independent: Sample data (concentration mol/dm³, initial g, final g): 0.0: 2.00, 2.30; 0.2: 2.00, 2.12; 0.4: 2.00, 1.96; 0.6: 2.00, 1.74; 0.8: 2.00, 1.60. Calculate each percentage change and plot the graph.
Use your graph to estimate the concentration of the potato cell contents. Explain your method. (3 marks)
Explain what happens to a red blood cell placed in distilled water. (3 marks)
exit: Define osmosis.
A cylinder loses mass in a sugar solution. Is the solution more or less concentrated than the cell contents?
lessons.homework: Write a short method for the potato practical, including the independent, dependent and control variables, and one safety point.
lessons.send: SEND: step-by-step calculation frame for percentage change. EAL: diagram of the cell with labelled arrows for water movement. Stretch: explain why the line of best fit is a better indicator of the zero point than a single data point.

lessons.title: Triple only: Culturing microorganisms
objectives: Describe aseptic technique for culturing microorganisms safely
Calculate the number of bacteria after a given number of divisions
Calculate the area of a zone of inhibition to compare antibiotics or antiseptics

keywords.def: methods that prevent unwanted microorganisms contaminating a culture or the person
simple cell division of bacteria that produces two daughter cells
a jelly containing nutrients on which microorganisms are grown
the clear area around an antibiotic disc where bacteria cannot grow

starter: Name the type of cell division in body cells.
State two features of bacterial cells.
Why is it important to repeat measurements in an experiment?

teach.heading: Growing bacteria in a lab
bullets: Bacteria are grown on nutrient agar in Petri dishes.
They can also be grown in warm nutrient broth.
Bacteria multiply by binary fission, as often as every 20 minutes.
Plenty of nutrients and warmth are needed.
teach.note: This content is Triple (separate) science only; Combined Trilogy pupils can treat it as enrichment. Ask: what does bacteria need to grow? Link to food spoilage and why we refrigerate food.

teach.heading: Aseptic technique
bullets: Sterilise Petri dishes and agar before use.
Pass inoculating loops through a flame to sterilise them.
Lid on at an angle, tape lightly, never fully seal.
Incubate at 25 °C in school to avoid growing human pathogens.
teach.note: SAFETY: this is a teacher-led practical or a video demonstration only. Never culture bacteria from the environment, hands or surfaces at home. The lid is taped (not sealed) so oxygen enters and anaerobic pathogens cannot grow. Incubation is at 25 °C in schools, whereas 37 °C would favour pathogenic bacteria.

teach.heading: Calculating bacterial numbers
bullets: Doubling time 20 minutes: one bacterium gives 2, 4, 8 ...
In 1 hour there are 3 divisions: 2³ = 8 bacteria.
In 2 hours there are 6 divisions: 2⁶ = 64 bacteria.
Number after n divisions = starting number × 2ⁿ.
teach.note: Work through a table of time against number. Ask: starting with 50 bacteria, how many after 100 minutes? (5 divisions, 50 × 32 = 1600). Practise standard form: 1.6 × 10³.

teach.heading: Testing antibiotics and antiseptics
bullets: Spread bacteria on agar, add discs soaked in different antibiotics.
Clear zone shows bacteria killed or unable to grow.
Area of zone = πr².
Larger zone means more effective against those bacteria.
teach.note: Worked example: a zone of diameter 14 mm has radius 7 mm, so area = 3.14 × 7² = 154 mm². Another zone of diameter 20 mm gives area = 3.14 × 10² = 314 mm². Stress that you must halve the diameter first. Ensure a control disc (water) is used.

teach.heading: Evaluating the investigation
bullets: Control: same volume of antiseptic, same agar thickness, same temperature.
Repeat to find a mean for each antiseptic.
Disc must be evenly spaced and not touching.
Dishes must be disposed of safely by autoclaving.
teach.note: Ask pupils to identify risks and how to reduce them. Link to the principle of avoiding harm to others and keeping clean. Mention the issue of antibiotic resistance as a motive for careful testing.

practice: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are there after 80 minutes starting with one?
Calculate the area of a zone of inhibition of diameter 18 mm. Use π = 3.14.
Explain why the Petri dish lid is taped at the sides but not completely sealed.
independent: A culture starts with 200 bacteria and the doubling time is 30 minutes. Calculate the number after 3 hours.
Antiseptic A has zone diameter 12 mm and antiseptic B has zone diameter 16 mm. Calculate both areas and say which is more effective. (4 marks)
Describe how aseptic technique prevents contamination. (4 marks)
exit: State why an incubator for school experiments is set to 25 °C.
Write the formula for the area of a circle.
lessons.homework: Write a clear method for testing two antiseptics, including three control variables and two safety precautions.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a laminated table for doubling calculations. EAL: images for each step of the aseptic technique. Stretch: explain why an antibiotic-resistant mutation might spread through a population of bacteria.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Atomic structure and the periodic table
lessons.title: Atoms, elements, compounds and mixtures
objectives: Distinguish between elements, compounds and mixtures
Write and interpret chemical formulae and symbol equations for simple changes
Choose a suitable method to separate a mixture and explain how it works

keywords.def: a substance made of only one type of atom
a substance of two or more elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions
two or more substances that are not chemically combined and can be separated by physical methods
separating a liquid from a solution or mixture by evaporating then condensing it

starter: Bismillah. State the three states of matter and one property of each.
What is the chemical symbol for sodium, oxygen and iron?
What is the difference between melting and dissolving?

teach.heading: Elements, compounds and mixtures
bullets: Element: one type of atom only, e.g. O₂, Fe, Na.
Compound: different atoms chemically bonded, e.g. H₂O, NaCl, CO₂.
Mixture: substances just mixed, not chemically bonded, e.g. air, seawater.
A compound has different properties from its elements.
teach.note: Hold up three particle diagrams (all same atom; two atom types joined; two atom types mixed but not joined) and ask pupils to classify. Misconception: air is a compound - it is a mixture of gases, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Sodium chloride is not like sodium (reactive metal) or chlorine (poisonous gas).

teach.heading: Filtration and crystallisation
bullets: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.
Crystallisation: heat solution to reduce volume, then cool for crystals.
Evaporation to dryness can work for a salt that does not decompose.
Example: separating salt from rock salt (salt and sand).
teach.note: Talk through rock salt: grind, dissolve in warm water, filter (sand stays on paper), heat filtrate in an evaporating basin until crystals start to form, then leave to cool. Online delivery: teacher demo or video; at home, adults only for hot water. Link: early Muslim scholars refined crystallisation and distillation in their laboratories, which later shaped chemistry.

teach.heading: Simple and fractional distillation
bullets: Simple distillation: pure solvent from a solution, e.g. water from salt water.
Fractional distillation: separates liquids with different boiling points.
Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C.
Ethanol evaporates first, then condenses and is collected.
teach.note: Draw the apparatus: flask, thermometer, condenser with water in at the bottom and out at the top, collecting beaker. Ask: why does the thermometer sit at the neck? To measure the temperature of the vapour. Remind pupils that this is a Bunsen burner or hot plate demonstration only. Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation in industry.

teach.heading: Chromatography
bullets: Separates mixtures of soluble substances, such as inks and dyes.
Draw the pencil start line, spot the sample, dip below the line.
The solvent rises, carrying substances different distances.
Pure substances give one spot.
teach.note: Pencil is used because ink would dissolve and run with the solvent. Home option: filter paper and water with felt-tip pens is safe; coffee filters are ideal. Ask pupils to predict how a mixture of three dyes appears: three spots at different heights. Rf calculations come later in the course.

teach.heading: Choosing a method
bullets: Insoluble solid from liquid: filtration.
Soluble solid from solution: crystallisation.
Solvent from solution: simple distillation.
Liquids with different boiling points: fractional distillation.
teach.note: Give a decision-tree on screen and rehearse with three scenarios: muddy water, ink colours, and a mixture of ethanol and water. Remind pupils that mixtures are separated by physical processes, not chemical reactions, because no new substances form.

practice: Classify as element, compound or mixture: sea water, carbon dioxide, iron, brass, hydrogen peroxide.
Name the best separation method for: (a) sand from water, (b) ethanol from water, (c) the dyes in black ink.
Explain why a pencil line is used on a chromatography paper rather than ink.
independent: Describe how you would obtain pure water from salty water. Include a labelled diagram. (4 marks)
Describe how to separate rock salt into sand and salt crystals. (5 marks)
Explain why fractional distillation can separate ethanol and water but filtration cannot. (2 marks)
exit: Give one difference between a compound and a mixture.
Which method separates an insoluble solid from a liquid?
lessons.homework: Using a coffee filter and washable pens at home, carry out a chromatography investigation with adult supervision and write down your observations.
lessons.send: SEND: sort cards for elements/compounds/mixtures with pictures. EAL: bilingual glossary for filtration, crystallisation and distillation. Stretch: explain why distilling a mixture of ethanol and water cannot give 100 % pure ethanol.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Atomic structure and the periodic table
lessons.title: Developing models of the atom
objectives: Describe the plum pudding model and why it was replaced by the nuclear model
Explain the results of the alpha particle scattering experiment
State how Bohr and Chadwick improved the model

keywords.def: the tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons
a negatively charged particle that orbits the nucleus in shells
an uncharged particle in the nucleus discovered by Chadwick
a simplified explanation of how something works that can be tested and changed with new evidence

starter: Name the three sub-atomic particles.
What does 'evidence' mean in science?
Why do scientists change theories?

teach.heading: Early ideas: Dalton and Thomson
bullets: Before 1800: atoms thought to be tiny, indivisible spheres.
John Dalton (early 1800s): atoms of an element are identical solid spheres.
Electron discovered by J. J. Thomson in 1897.
Plum pudding model: negative electrons in a ball of positive charge.
teach.note: Ask pupils: what does a 'model' do? It helps us explain and predict. Emphasise that each model was reasonable given the evidence at that time. Introduce the idea of science being a continuing conversation and that good scientists admit when they were wrong, in line with truthfulness.

teach.heading: Rutherford's alpha scattering
bullets: Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil by Geiger and Marsden.
Most passed straight through: atoms are mostly empty space.
Some were deflected: the centre is positive.
A very few bounced back: a tiny, dense nucleus.
teach.note: Use the 'firing bullets at tissue paper' analogy: a few bounce back, which was astonishing. Show a diagram with the three outcomes. In the exam, link each observation to a conclusion: 'most pass through, so mostly empty space'.

teach.heading: The nuclear model
bullets: Rutherford (1911) proposed a small positive nucleus with electrons around it.
Radius of an atom is about 0.1 nm (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m).
Nucleus radius is about 1/10 000 of the atom.
Most of the mass is in the nucleus.
teach.note: Scale it: if the atom were a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea at the centre. Check pupils can read standard form. Misconception: electrons are not tiny planets orbiting in circles; shells are a useful model.

teach.heading: Bohr and Chadwick
bullets: Niels Bohr: electrons orbit at fixed distances in shells.
Calculations matched observations of how atoms emit light.
Protons were identified as positive particles in the nucleus.
James Chadwick (about 1932) provided evidence for neutrons.
teach.note: Explain that Bohr's shell idea explains why electrons do not spiral into the nucleus. The existence of neutrons explained why atoms are heavier than the number of protons suggest. Ask: why were neutrons hard to detect? (They have no charge.)

teach.heading: How science develops
bullets: New evidence leads to a revised model.
Other scientists check and repeat experiments (peer review).
A model is kept only while it explains all the evidence.
Honesty with data is essential.
teach.note: Link to the Islamic ethic of seeking knowledge: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that whoever follows a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise (Sahih Muslim). Ask pupils to write one sentence on why peer review matters.

practice: Put these models in order of development: nuclear model, plum pudding model, Bohr model, solid sphere.
In the gold foil experiment, what did it tell scientists when a few alpha particles bounced back?
Why was the plum pudding model abandoned?
independent: Draw and label the plum pudding model and the nuclear model, and give one difference.
Explain how the results of the alpha scattering experiment changed the model of the atom. (4 marks)
An atom has radius 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and its nucleus has radius 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m. How many times larger is the atom than the nucleus?
exit: Which scientist discovered the electron?
What does 'most alpha particles passed through' tell us about the atom?
lessons.homework: Create a timeline of five scientists who developed the atomic model with one line on each contribution.
lessons.send: SEND: timeline strip to cut and sequence. EAL: simplified language with diagrams of the experiment. Stretch: explain why the observation that a few alphas are deflected by more than 90° could not be explained by the plum pudding model.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Atomic structure and the periodic table
lessons.title: Sub-atomic particles, isotopes and relative atomic mass
objectives: State the relative charge and mass of protons, neutrons and electrons
Use atomic number and mass number to find the number of each particle
Calculate relative atomic mass from isotope abundance

keywords.def: the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom
the total number of protons and neutrons in an atom
atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
the average mass of atoms of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom

starter: Who proposed the nuclear model of the atom?
Where are the electrons in an atom?
What does the term 'neutral' mean for an atom?

teach.heading: Protons, neutrons, electrons
bullets: Proton: relative mass 1, relative charge +1.
Neutron: relative mass 1, charge 0.
Electron: relative mass very small (about 1/1836), charge −1.
Atoms are neutral: protons equal electrons.
teach.note: Quick table on screen. Check that pupils can say why atoms have no overall charge. Misconception: the electron mass is 'zero'; AQA accepts 'very small' or 1/1836, and calling it negligible.

teach.heading: Reading the periodic table
bullets: Atomic number (smaller) = protons = electrons.
Mass number (larger) = protons + neutrons.
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
Example: Sodium-23 has 11 protons, 11 electrons, 12 neutrons.
teach.note: Work through three examples live: carbon-12 (6, 6, 6), oxygen-16 (8, 8, 8), chlorine-35 (17, 17, 18). Warn: in some periodic tables the larger number is the relative atomic mass, which may not be a whole number.

teach.heading: Isotopes
bullets: Isotopes have the same protons but different neutrons.
Chemical properties are the same, because electrons are the same.
Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon.
Isotopes have different masses.
teach.note: Use cards to show Cl-35 and Cl-37. Ask: what is the same and what is different? Carbon-14 is radioactive and used for dating, which pupils will meet in physics. Stress 'same atomic number, different mass number'.

teach.heading: Relative atomic mass
bullets: Relative atomic mass is the weighted average of isotope masses.
RAM = sum of (isotope mass × abundance) ÷ 100.
Chlorine: 75 % Cl-35 and 25 % Cl-37.
teach.note: Show the working: 2625 + 925 = 3550, then ÷ 100 = 35.5. Second example: boron, 20 % B-10 and 80 % B-11, gives (200 + 880) ÷ 100 = 10.8. Explain why the answer is not a whole number (it is an average). Give a calculator reminder to use brackets.

teach.heading: Ions and exam technique
bullets: Ions form when atoms gain or lose electrons.
Na⁺: 11 protons, 10 electrons.
Cl⁻: 17 protons, 18 electrons.
Always show working in calculation questions.
teach.note: Ask: does the number of protons change when an ion forms? No, so it is still the same element. Remind pupils that for 'calculate' questions marks are for the formula, substitution and answer with units.

practice: State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in aluminium-27 (atomic number 13).
Explain why the isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties.
Magnesium has isotopes Mg-24 (79 %), Mg-25 (10 %) and Mg-26 (11 %). Calculate the relative atomic mass.
independent: Complete a table for: Li-7 (atomic number 3), F-19 (9), K-39 (19), Ca-40 (20), with protons, neutrons, electrons.
Copper has two isotopes: Cu-63 (69 %) and Cu-65 (31 %). Calculate the relative atomic mass to 1 decimal place. (3 marks)
Explain why carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes. (2 marks)
exit: How many neutrons are in an atom of fluorine-19 (atomic number 9)?
What is an isotope?
lessons.homework: Write out a table for the first 20 elements showing protons and electrons, and complete five relative atomic mass questions.
lessons.send: SEND: coloured bead model to show particle counts. EAL: pre-teach the prefix 'iso-'. Stretch: explain why chlorine's relative atomic mass is 35.5 but no chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Atomic structure and the periodic table
lessons.title: Electronic structure and the modern periodic table
objectives: Write electronic configurations for the first 20 elements
Explain how position in the periodic table relates to electronic structure
Compare the positions of metals and non-metals

keywords.def: an energy level in an atom where electrons are found
a vertical column of the periodic table; elements have the same number of outer electrons
a horizontal row of the periodic table; shows the number of electron shells
the electrons in the highest occupied energy level; they determine reactions

starter: What is the atomic number of sodium?
How many protons are in an oxygen atom?
What do the numbers at the top and bottom of an element box show?

teach.heading: Filling the shells
bullets: First shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons.
Second and third shells hold up to 8 electrons.
Fill the lowest energy level first.
Example: sodium (11) is 2,8,1; chlorine (17) is 2,8,7.
teach.note: Model the first 20 elements. Common errors: putting 3 electrons in the first shell; or not completing the second shell before starting the third. Practise drawing shell diagrams with crosses for electrons.

teach.heading: Reading groups and periods
bullets: Group number = number of outer-shell electrons.
Period number = number of occupied shells.
Group 0 (8 or 2 outer electrons) is full: unreactive.
Example: calcium is 2,8,8,2: Group 2, Period 4.
teach.note: Display a blank periodic table and colour code Groups 1, 2, 7 and 0. Ask: what do all Group 1 elements have in common? (1 outer electron). Explain that this explains similar chemical properties in a group.

teach.heading: The periodic table today
bullets: Elements are arranged in order of atomic number.
Elements in a group have similar chemical properties.
Metals are to the left and in the middle.
Non-metals are to the right (and hydrogen).
teach.note: Highlight the staircase line that separates metals and non-metals. Ask pupils to find: 5 metals, 5 non-metals, one noble gas, one halogen. Explain that more than three quarters of the known elements are metals.

teach.heading: Metals, non-metals and ion formation
bullets: Metal atoms lose outer electrons to form positive ions.
Non-metal atoms gain or share electrons to complete a shell.
Na → Na⁺ + e⁻.
Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻.
teach.note: Link outer shell to reactivity: atoms react to get a full outer shell like a noble gas. This is a useful preview of bonding in the next unit. Check understanding: does sodium gain or lose an electron? Why?

teach.heading: Properties of metals and non-metals
bullets: Metals: shiny, good conductors, malleable, ductile, high melting point.
Non-metals: dull, poor conductors, brittle if solid, low melting points.
Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic.
Exceptions exist: graphite conducts, mercury is liquid.
teach.note: Give pupils a pile of statement cards to sort. Exam tip: 'give two properties of metals' needs specific properties, e.g. conducts electricity, not 'strong' alone. Use the exceptions to show nuance.

practice: Write the electronic structure of: oxygen (8), magnesium (12), aluminium (13), argon (18).
State the group and period of phosphorus (15).
Explain why the elements lithium, sodium and potassium have similar chemical properties.
independent: Draw shell diagrams of the first 20 elements and colour-code by group.
Explain why neon is unreactive but fluorine is reactive. (3 marks)
Predict the electronic structure of the ion Mg²⁺ and the ion O²⁻. (2 marks)
exit: What is the electronic structure of chlorine?
What does the group number of an element tell you?
lessons.homework: Complete a periodic table sheet colour-coding groups, adding electronic structures for the first 20 elements.
lessons.send: SEND: use pre-drawn shell templates and counters. EAL: simple sentences 'Sodium is in Group 1 because...' Stretch: explain why the third shell is sometimes drawn with 8 electrons for argon yet can hold more.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Atomic structure and the periodic table
lessons.title: Developing the periodic table: Newlands, Mendeleev and transition metals
objectives: Describe how Newlands and Mendeleev arranged the elements
Explain why Mendeleev's table was accepted
State typical properties of transition metals

keywords.def: Russian chemist who arranged elements by atomic weight in groups and left gaps for undiscovered elements
a metal in the central block of the periodic table, with high melting points and coloured compounds
a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up
a statement of what will happen, based on a theory

starter: How many outer electrons does a Group 2 element have?
Describe the position of metals in the periodic table.
What is an atomic number?

teach.heading: Before the periodic table
bullets: Early chemists sorted elements by properties and by atomic weight.
Protons, electrons and isotopes were not yet known.
Atomic weight (relative atomic mass) was the only measure.
Many elements were still undiscovered.
teach.note: Set context: by 1860 about 60 elements were known. Ask pupils how they would organise a pile of unknown objects. Introduce the idea that patterns can help predict. Early Muslim chemists classified substances by properties too, e.g. spirits, metals and stones, a tradition of careful classification.

teach.heading: Newlands' Law of Octaves
bullets: 1864: Newlands arranged elements by atomic weight.
Every eighth element had similar properties, like octaves in music.
The pattern broke down after calcium.
Newlands put different elements in the same group, and was criticised.
teach.note: Explain that the idea was a useful step but incomplete, because it did not leave gaps for elements not yet discovered. Many scientists mocked him; later the pattern was understood. Reflect on adab in disagreement: criticise ideas respectfully.

teach.heading: Mendeleev's table (1869)
bullets: Arranged by atomic weight but kept chemical similarity in groups.
Swapped the order of some elements so they fitted their group.
Left gaps for undiscovered elements.
Predicted properties of the missing elements, e.g. germanium.
teach.note: Key: Mendeleev's predictions were later confirmed when gallium and germanium were discovered, convincing scientists. Later, isotopes and atomic number explained why switching a few elements was justified (e.g. iodine and tellurium). Today's table is ordered by atomic number.

teach.heading: Transition metals
bullets: Found in the central block between Groups 2 and 3.
Higher melting points and densities than Group 1.
Strong, hard and less reactive than Group 1 metals.
Form coloured compounds and ions with different charges.
teach.note: Show examples: copper sulfate (blue), iron(III) compounds (brown/orange), potassium manganate(VII) (purple). Mention iron as a catalyst in the Haber process and platinum in catalytic converters. Compare with sodium (soft, low melting point). Note mercury is a liquid, an exception to the high melting point.

teach.heading: Explaining and evaluating
bullets: Good evidence: successful predictions convinced scientists.
Compare Newlands and Mendeleev using specific features.
A scientific theory must be testable.
Link properties to atomic structure when asked.
teach.note: Practise a 6-mark style plan: Newlands - ordered by atomic weight, octaves, no gaps; Mendeleev - gaps, predictions, grouped by properties; conclusion - why the second won support. Pupils write a plan in bullet form first.

practice: State two ways Mendeleev's periodic table differed from Newlands' octaves.
Give three properties of transition metals.
Why did the discovery of germanium support Mendeleev's table?
independent: Compare transition metals with Group 1 metals in a table covering: melting point, density, hardness, reactivity.
Explain how Mendeleev's periodic table was an improvement on earlier tables. (4 marks)
Describe two uses of transition metals or their compounds. (2 marks)
exit: What did Mendeleev leave in his table that Newlands did not?
Give one property that transition metals have but Group 1 metals do not.
lessons.homework: Research the discovery of gallium or germanium and write six lines on how its properties matched Mendeleev's predictions.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a sequencing activity with cards. EAL: key words with translations. Stretch: explain why ordering by relative atomic mass fails for tellurium and iodine and how atomic number resolved this.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Atomic structure and the periodic table
lessons.title: Group 0 and Group 1: noble gases and alkali metals
objectives: Explain why noble gases are unreactive and describe their trends
Describe the reactions of alkali metals with water and write equations
Explain the trend in reactivity down Group 1 using electronic structure

keywords.def: an unreactive Group 0 element with a full outer shell of electrons
a Group 1 metal that reacts with water to form an alkaline hydroxide solution
how easily and quickly an element reacts
a compound containing OH⁻ ions; alkaline solutions contain them

starter: What is the electronic structure of sodium?
How many electrons does a Group 1 atom have in its outer shell?
State two properties of metals.

teach.heading: Group 0: the noble gases
bullets: Full outer shells: helium has 2, others have 8.
Unreactive, so they do not easily form molecules.
Exist as single atoms (monatomic) and are colourless.
Boiling points increase down the group.
teach.note: Uses: helium in balloons and airships (not flammable), argon in filament lamps to stop the filament burning, neon in signs. Ask: why would hydrogen be more dangerous than helium in balloons? Because hydrogen is flammable.

teach.heading: Group 1: the alkali metals
bullets: Lithium, sodium and potassium: one outer electron.
Soft, shiny metals with low density and low melting points.
Stored in oil, because they react with air and water.
They form 1+ ions in compounds.
teach.note: Compare with transition metals from the last lesson. Explain that they can be cut with a knife; the freshly cut surface quickly tarnishes in air. Show the periodic table with group labels. Misconception: alkali metals do not dissolve, they react with water to form alkaline solutions.

teach.heading: Reaction with water
bullets: Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen.
2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.
Lithium fizzes, sodium melts into a ball, potassium burns with a lilac flame.
The solution is alkaline (universal indicator turns purple).
teach.note: SAFETY: demonstrate with video or teacher demonstration behind a safety screen with a very small piece, goggles, and a trough. These are never to be done at home. Balance the equation with pupils line by line. Ask: how can we test the gas given off? Lit splint gives a squeaky pop.

teach.heading: Trend in reactivity
bullets: Reactivity increases down the group.
Lithium < sodium < potassium < rubidium < caesium.
Larger atoms: outer electron is further from the nucleus.
Weaker attraction, so the electron is lost more easily.
teach.note: Ask pupils to explain step by step: shell number increases, electron further from nucleus, more shielding, less attraction, easier to lose, more reactive. Provide sentence stems. Also melting points decrease down the group, so potassium melts more easily than lithium.

teach.heading: Exam questions on the trend
bullets: Predict: rubidium reacts more vigorously than potassium.
Explain using position of the outer electron.
Include the product formulae in equations.
Use state symbols if asked: (s), (l), (g), (aq).
teach.note: Work an example: 'Rubidium is below potassium. Predict its reaction with water and write the equation: 2Rb + 2H₂O → 2RbOH + H₂.' Encourage pupils to use pattern recognition when writing equations for other Group 1 metals.

practice: Write the word and balanced symbol equation for lithium with water.
Explain why helium is used in airships rather than hydrogen.
Describe the observations when potassium is added to water.
independent: Explain why caesium is more reactive than lithium. (3 marks)
Predict two differences between the reaction of sodium and the reaction of potassium with water. (2 marks)
Write a balanced equation for potassium reacting with water and state the pH range of the solution formed.
exit: What is the formula of the hydroxide formed when sodium reacts with water?
Why do noble gases not react easily?
lessons.homework: Create a table of properties and trends for Group 1 and Group 0 with at least two explanations using electronic structure.
lessons.send: SEND: equation balancing using paper counters. EAL: provide sentence starters for explaining the trend. Stretch: explain why francium would be expected to be the most reactive Group 1 metal.

lessons.unit: Chemistry: Atomic structure and the periodic table
lessons.title: Group 7: the halogens and displacement reactions
objectives: Describe the physical properties and trends of the halogens
Explain why reactivity decreases down Group 7
Predict and write equations for halogen displacement reactions

keywords.def: an element in Group 7 with seven outer electrons that exists as diatomic molecules
a reaction where a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound
made of molecules containing two atoms, e.g. Cl₂
a compound of a halogen with another element, e.g. sodium chloride

starter: Write the electronic structure of chlorine.
What happens to the reactivity of Group 1 metals down the group, and why?
What is the charge on a chloride ion?

teach.heading: Physical properties of halogens
bullets: Chlorine: pale green gas. Bromine: red-brown liquid. Iodine: grey solid.
They exist as diatomic molecules: F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.
Melting and boiling points increase down the group.
They are poisonous non-metals.
teach.note: SAFETY: chlorine and bromine are toxic and corrosive. Show video or sealed sample images only. Iodine gives a purple vapour on heating. Ask pupils to predict astatine's state (a dark solid). Remind them the trend in boiling point is opposite from Group 1 melting points.

teach.heading: Reactions of halogens
bullets: Halogens form ionic compounds with metals, with 1− ions.
Example: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
With non-metals they form covalent compounds, e.g. HCl.
Each halogen atom gains one electron to fill its outer shell.
teach.note: Draw a dot-and-cross for sodium chloride. Ask: why do halogens gain an electron? Because they need one more to complete the outer shell. Link to electronic structure in the previous lessons.

teach.heading: Trend in reactivity
bullets: Reactivity decreases down Group 7.
Fluorine is the most reactive halogen.
Outer shell nearer to the nucleus in smaller atoms.
Stronger attraction, so an electron is gained more easily.
teach.note: Contrast with Group 1: metals lose electrons so larger atoms are more reactive; halogens gain electrons so smaller atoms are more reactive. This is a very commonly tested 'explain' question. Use the sentence stem: 'As you go down the group the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so the attraction to an incoming electron is weaker...'.

teach.heading: Displacement reactions
bullets: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from a salt.
Cl₂ + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br₂.
Chlorine water + potassium iodide gives a brown solution of iodine.
Bromine cannot displace chlorine from sodium chloride.
teach.note: Give a results table to complete (chlorine, bromine and iodine water against potassium chloride, bromide and iodide): chlorine displaces bromine and iodine; bromine displaces iodine only; iodine displaces nothing. Practical is a demonstration or video, since halogen solutions are hazardous. Use predict-observe-explain.

teach.heading: Writing and explaining equations
bullets: Balance atoms and use diatomic formulae for halogens.
Ionic equation: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.
Chlorine gains electrons: it is reduced.
Link reactivity order to electronic structure in explanations.
teach.note: Higher tier pupils may consider the ionic equation. Foundation tier should be fluent with the word and symbol equations. Reflect: patterns in nature let us predict, a theme in Qur'an 3:190-191 where signs are for those who reflect.

practice: Complete: chlorine + potassium bromide → ___ + ___. Write a balanced symbol equation.
State the physical state and colour of bromine at room temperature.
Predict whether iodine will react with sodium chloride solution and give a reason.
independent: Explain why fluorine is more reactive than iodine. (3 marks)
A student adds bromine water to potassium chloride, potassium iodide and potassium bromide solutions. Predict the result in each case.
Compare the trends in reactivity in Group 1 and Group 7 and explain the difference. (4 marks)
exit: What is a displacement reaction?
Name the product when chlorine displaces iodine from sodium iodide.
lessons.homework: Write a revision mind map for the periodic table unit covering Groups 0, 1 and 7 and the history of the atom.
lessons.send: SEND: results grid with colour clues. EAL: key phrase bank 'more reactive than', 'displaces'. Stretch: predict the reaction of astatine with potassium iodide and justify your answer.

lessons.title: Circuit symbols, current, charge and potential difference
objectives: Draw and interpret circuit diagrams using standard symbols
Use Q = It to calculate charge, current or time
Define potential difference and connect an ammeter and voltmeter correctly

keywords.def: the rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A)
the energy transferred per unit charge, measured in volts (V)
a property of matter that experiences force in an electric field, measured in coulombs (C)
a device connected in series that measures current

starter: Bismillah. Name three electrical appliances at home and the energy they transfer.
What do we call a material that lets electricity flow easily?
What are the units of energy?

teach.heading: Circuit symbols
bullets: Cell, battery, switch (open and closed), lamp, fuse.
Fixed resistor, variable resistor, LED, diode.
LDR, thermistor, ammeter (A) and voltmeter (V).
Draw straight lines, with no gaps in the circuit.
teach.note: Show all symbols on screen and play a quick-fire recognition game. Exam tip: draw circuits with a ruler and make sure the voltmeter is outside the main circuit loop. Misconception: a 'battery' is two or more cells, so the symbol with several lines represents a battery.

teach.heading: Current and charge
bullets: Current is the rate of flow of charge: Q = I t.
Q in coulombs (C), I in amps (A), t in seconds (s).
In a metal wire, free electrons carry the charge.
Current is the same at every point in a series loop.
teach.note: Worked example: 3 A for 4 seconds: Q = 3 x 4 = 12 C. Second: Q = 180 C, t = 30 s gives I = 180 ÷ 30 = 6 A. Emphasise convert minutes into seconds (e.g. 2 minutes is 120 s). Conventional current is drawn from + to −, but electrons actually move from − to +.

teach.heading: Potential difference
bullets: Potential difference is the work done per unit of charge.
V = E ÷ Q: volts = joules per coulomb.
A 12 V cell gives 12 J to each coulomb of charge.
Measured with a voltmeter connected in parallel.
teach.note: Water analogy: pump gives energy to water (the cell raises the charge's energy); the pipe's resistance drains it. Example: 240 J transferred by 20 C of charge; V = 240 ÷ 20 = 12 V. Misconception: current is not used up; energy is transferred, but charge continues round the loop.

teach.heading: Connecting meters
bullets: Ammeter goes in series: in the circuit, in the loop.
Voltmeter goes in parallel across the component.
An ideal ammeter has very low resistance.
A voltmeter has very high resistance.
teach.note: Draw a lamp circuit with both meters and ask pupils to trace the loop with a finger. If a voltmeter is wired in series it would block the current. Use the PhET 'Circuit Construction Kit: DC' simulation so pupils can build circuits safely online.

teach.heading: Safe and accurate practice
bullets: Use low voltages in school and avoid water near electricity.
Never experiment with mains electricity at home.
Read meter scales carefully and check the zero error.
Record values with units.
teach.note: Islamic ethic: preserve life and avoid harm to oneself and others. All electrical practical work online uses a simulation or teacher demonstration with batteries; pupils must never open plugs or experiment with sockets at home.

practice: A current of 0.5 A flows for 2 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows.
A battery transfers 90 J of energy to 15 C of charge. Calculate the potential difference.
Draw a circuit with a cell, switch, lamp and an ammeter in series, and a voltmeter across the lamp.
independent: Use the PhET Circuit Construction Kit to build a series circuit with one battery and two bulbs; record the current at three points. Describe your findings.
Calculate: (a) charge when 2.5 A flows for 40 s, (b) time for 600 C to flow at 4 A, (c) energy transferred by 30 C moving through 6 V.
Explain why an ammeter must be connected in series and not in parallel. (2 marks)
exit: State the equation linking charge, current and time.
What is the unit of potential difference?
lessons.homework: Complete a worksheet of six circuit diagrams with missing symbols and four Q = I t calculations.
lessons.send: SEND: give a symbol bank to copy and use a colour code for series loops. EAL: label meters with arrows 'in series'/'in parallel'. Stretch: show that 1 V = 1 J/C and use it to calculate the energy in a 5 A, 230 V appliance in one second.

lessons.title: Resistance, Ohm's law and the required practical
objectives: Use V = I R to calculate potential difference, current or resistance
Explain what affects the resistance of a wire
Describe and analyse the required practical on resistance and wire length

keywords.def: a measure of how much a component opposes the flow of current, in ohms (Ω)
a component whose current is directly proportional to p.d. at constant temperature
a resistor whose resistance can be changed to control current
the variable you change in an investigation

starter: Calculate the charge from 3 A flowing for 10 s.
Where is a voltmeter connected?
Convert 2.5 kΩ into ohms.

teach.heading: Resistance and V = I R
bullets: Resistance opposes the flow of current.
V = I R; I = V ÷ R; R = V ÷ I.
Resistance is in ohms (Ω).
Increasing resistance reduces the current for the same p.d.
teach.note: Use a triangle with V at the top. Worked example: 6 V across a 12 Ω resistor gives I = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 A. Second: a lamp has 0.25 A at 3.0 V: R = 3.0 ÷ 0.25 = 12 Ω. Insist on units.

teach.heading: Ohmic conductors
bullets: At constant temperature, current is directly proportional to p.d.
The I-V graph is a straight line through the origin.
A fixed resistor is an ohmic conductor.
Resistance stays constant.
teach.note: Show a graph with a straight line. Ask: what would the gradient tell you? For I against V, the gradient is 1/R, so a steeper line means a smaller resistance. Many pupils mix this up; contrast with V against I where gradient equals R.

teach.heading: Required practical: resistance of a wire
bullets: Connect a wire, ammeter in series and voltmeter across the wire.
Change the length of wire between the crocodile clips.
Measure V and I for lengths such as 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 cm.
Calculate R = V ÷ I and plot R against length.
teach.note: SAFETY AND ONLINE DELIVERY: use a low-voltage supply or a single 1.5 V cell, and switch off between readings because wires can get hot. At home use the PhET 'Resistance in a Wire' or 'Ohm's Law' simulations, or the teacher live-streams the experiment. Never use mains. Variables: independent - length; dependent - resistance; control - wire material, diameter, temperature, voltage.

teach.heading: Analysing sample data
bullets: Sample data at 1.5 V: 20 cm gives 1.50 A.
40 cm gives 0.75 A and 60 cm gives 0.50 A.
Resistance is directly proportional to length.
Doubling the length doubles the resistance.
teach.note: Ask pupils to calculate R from each pair of readings and sketch the graph: a straight line through the origin. Explain why: more length means more collisions between electrons and the metal ions in the wire. Thicker wire has a lower resistance, since more paths are available for electrons.

teach.heading: Evaluating the practical
bullets: Keep the current low to avoid heating the wire.
Repeat readings and calculate a mean.
Check for zero error on meters.
Use a longer wire for more points on the graph.
teach.note: Pupils often forget that heating changes the resistance, so the wire would stop being a fair test. Ask: how does a variable resistor help? It controls the current. Link to honesty in recording results, even if they do not fit the expected pattern.

practice: A 9 V battery is connected to a 45 Ω resistor. Calculate the current.
A component has a current of 0.4 A when the p.d. is 2.0 V. Calculate its resistance.
Explain why doubling the length of a wire doubles its resistance.
independent: Using the sample data, calculate the resistance for 80 cm (V = 1.5 V, I = 0.375 A) and 100 cm (I = 0.30 A), plot a graph, and describe the relationship.
Write a method for the required practical, including variables to control. (4 marks)
Explain why the wire should not be left connected for long periods. (2 marks)
exit: Write the equation linking potential difference, current and resistance.
What is the relationship between wire length and resistance?
lessons.homework: Complete five V = I R calculations and write a conclusion for the wire practical, mentioning direct proportionality.
lessons.send: SEND: step-by-step table to record readings and calculate R. EAL: pre-teach 'directly proportional'. Stretch: predict how resistance changes if wire diameter is doubled and explain using the cross-sectional area.

lessons.title: I-V characteristics: lamps, diodes, LDRs and thermistors
objectives: Describe and sketch I-V graphs for a resistor, filament lamp and diode
Explain the behaviour of LDRs and thermistors
Describe how to carry out the I-V characteristics required practical

keywords.def: a lamp whose thin wire heats up when current flows, increasing its resistance
a component that allows current in one direction only
light-dependent resistor; its resistance decreases as light intensity increases
a resistor whose resistance changes with temperature; for the NTC type it decreases as temperature rises

starter: Write the equation V = I R as a triangle.
Calculate the resistance if 2 A flows when 10 V is applied.
What does 'directly proportional' mean?

teach.heading: The required practical
bullets: Circuit: cell or power supply, variable resistor, ammeter in series.
Voltmeter across the component being tested.
Change the p.d. with the variable resistor and record I.
Swap the connections to take readings in the reverse direction.
teach.note: SAFETY AND ONLINE DELIVERY: use a low-voltage supply (up to about 6 V); do not exceed the lamp rating. Online option: PhET 'Circuit Construction Kit' with a lamp and diode, or teacher demonstration with a document camera. Insist that a diode must always have a series protective resistor in a real circuit or it could be damaged.

teach.heading: Filament lamp
bullets: I-V graph is a curve: gradient decreases as p.d. increases.
Current increases less than proportionally.
Temperature of filament rises, so resistance increases.
Atoms vibrate more, so electrons collide more often.
teach.note: Sample data: at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 V the currents are 0.20, 0.32, 0.41, 0.48 and 0.54 A, so R = 5.0, 6.3, 7.3, 8.3 and 9.3 Ω. Ask pupils to calculate these. The explanation uses ions vibrating more and more collisions: this is often a 3-mark question.

teach.heading: Diode
bullets: Current flows in one direction only (forward).
Resistance is very high in the reverse direction.
Forward current starts after a threshold of about 0.6 V.
LEDs emit light when current flows through them.
teach.note: Draw the graph: nearly no current until about 0.6 V forward, then a rapid increase; zero in the reverse direction. Applications: LEDs in displays; diodes in a.c. adapters. Misconception: a diode does not make current go faster; it only controls the direction.

teach.heading: LDRs and thermistors
bullets: LDR: resistance falls as light intensity increases.
Thermistor (NTC): resistance falls as temperature increases.
LDR uses: automatic street lights, burglar alarms.
Thermistor uses: thermostats, fire alarms.
teach.note: Show graphs of resistance against light intensity and against temperature. Ask pupils to design a night-light: the LDR resistance rises in the dark, so the voltage across it rises and switches on the lamp. This is application-level questioning typical of higher marks.

teach.heading: Interpreting graphs
bullets: At any point on an I-V graph, R = V ÷ I.
A steep I-V line means low resistance.
Describe the shape, then explain the cause.
Quote data from the graph with units.
teach.note: Practise reading values from a graph and calculating R at 2 V for each component. Common error: reading the gradient of a curved I-V graph as the resistance; always use R = V ÷ I at a point.

practice: Use the sample data to calculate the resistance of the filament lamp at 5 V.
Sketch the I-V graph for a diode and label the threshold.
State what happens to the resistance of an LDR when light intensity increases.
independent: Plot the sample data for the filament lamp and describe the shape of the graph.
Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the current increases. (3 marks)
Describe how a thermistor could be used in a fire alarm. (2 marks)
exit: Which component only allows current in one direction?
What happens to a thermistor's resistance as temperature increases?
lessons.homework: Draw four I-V graphs (resistor, lamp, diode, thermistor resistance-temperature) with a one-line explanation under each.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-printed graph axes and key phrases. EAL: component picture cards with names. Stretch: explain how a potential divider using an LDR can switch a lamp on in the dark.

lessons.title: Series and parallel circuits
objectives: Compare current, potential difference and resistance in series and parallel circuits
Calculate total resistance in series circuits
Explain why household circuits are wired in parallel

keywords.def: a circuit with one loop, so the same current flows through every component
a circuit with branches; the p.d. is the same across each branch
the single resistance that could replace all the components with the same effect
a separate path for current in a parallel circuit

starter: Where do you connect an ammeter?
Calculate current if V = 12 V and R = 4 Ω.
What happens to a filament lamp's resistance as it heats up?

teach.heading: Series circuits
bullets: One loop only: the current is the same everywhere.
Total p.d. of the supply is shared between components.
Total resistance = R₁ + R₂ + ...
If one component breaks, the whole circuit stops.
teach.note: Worked example: a 3 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor in series have a total resistance of 9 Ω. With a 9 V cell, current = 9 ÷ 9 = 1 A. P.d. across the 3 Ω resistor = 1 x 3 = 3 V and across the 6 Ω resistor = 6 V; the p.d.s add to 9 V. Misconception: current is not shared in series; the p.d. is.

teach.heading: Parallel circuits
bullets: Branches: the p.d. across each branch equals the supply p.d.
Total current is the sum of the branch currents.
Adding a branch decreases the total resistance.
If one branch breaks, the others still work.
teach.note: Example: ammeter A₁ reads 0.9 A at the cell, one branch carries 0.6 A, so the other branch carries 0.3 A. Misconception: pupils think more branches means more resistance; actually more paths for current make total resistance smaller. Total resistance is smaller than the smallest branch.

teach.heading: Cells in series and parallel
bullets: Cells in series: add their p.d. (when pointing the same way).
Two 1.5 V cells in series give 3.0 V.
Cells in the opposite direction subtract their p.d.
Use series cells to increase the voltage.
teach.note: Quick check: a battery has three 1.5 V cells in series; what is its p.d.? (4.5 V). Include a cell reversed: 1.5 + 1.5 − 1.5 = 1.5 V. Stay with series cells at GCSE level.

teach.heading: Why are homes wired in parallel?
bullets: Each appliance gets the full mains p.d. of 230 V.
Each can be switched on and off independently.
A faulty appliance does not stop the others working.
Series would share voltage, so appliances would not work properly.
teach.note: Compare with old-fashioned series fairy lights where one broken bulb stops the whole string. Ask pupils to design a circuit with two lamps, each with its own switch, and a master switch. Practise drawing it.

teach.heading: Circuit rules summary
bullets: Series: I same, V shared, R adds.
Parallel: V same, I shares, R decreases.
Current into a junction equals current out.
State rules in words and numbers.
teach.note: Provide a summary table for pupils to complete. Emphasise exam skill: when calculating, label all quantities with the component name (e.g. V₁, I₂) and show equation V = I R each time. Use PhET to check predictions: build the circuits and compare with calculation.

practice: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 8 Ω are in series with a 6 V battery. Calculate the current and the p.d. across each resistor.
In a parallel circuit, the total current is 1.2 A and one branch carries 0.5 A. Find the other branch current.
Explain why adding a second identical lamp in parallel makes the total resistance smaller.
independent: Calculate the total resistance of 10 Ω, 20 Ω and 30 Ω resistors connected in series, and the current from a 12 V supply.
Draw a circuit diagram for two lamps in parallel, each with its own switch, powered by one cell.
Explain two advantages of wiring home lights in parallel. (2 marks)
exit: In a series circuit, what is the same at every point?
In a parallel circuit, what happens to the total current as more branches are added?
lessons.homework: Build a series and parallel circuit using a simulator, record meter readings, and write a short summary of the rules.
lessons.send: SEND: use colour-coded loops on circuit diagrams. EAL: key phrases 'the same in series', 'shared in parallel'. Stretch: calculate total resistance of two 6 Ω resistors in parallel (3 Ω) and explain the answer.

lessons.title: Mains electricity and domestic safety
objectives: Compare direct and alternating potential difference
Identify the live, neutral and earth wires and their colours
Explain how fuses and earthing protect users

keywords.def: current that repeatedly changes direction, as in UK mains at 50 Hz
current that flows in one direction only, as from a cell
