the wire carrying the alternating p.d. of 230 V, coloured brown
a safety wire connecting the metal case to the ground, coloured green and yellow

starter: Why are homes wired in parallel?
What are the units of frequency?
What can happen if too much current flows in a wire?

teach.heading: a.c. and d.c.
bullets: Direct current (d.c.) always flows in the same direction, e.g. from cells.
Alternating current (a.c.) repeatedly reverses direction.
UK mains is a.c. at 230 V and 50 Hz.
Oscilloscope traces show d.c. as a flat line, a.c. as a wave.
teach.note: Draw d.c. and a.c. traces. Ask pupils to find the period of a 50 Hz supply: 1/50 s = 0.02 s. Stress: the mains frequency is 50 Hz, meaning 50 complete cycles each second. Link to power stations: generators produce a.c.

teach.heading: The three-core cable
bullets: Live wire: brown, carries the alternating p.d. of 230 V.
Neutral wire: blue, completes the circuit, around 0 V.
Earth wire: green and yellow stripes, safety wire at 0 V.
The cable is insulated with plastic.
teach.note: Show a plug diagram with correct wire positions and fuse in the live side. Stress the earth wire does not carry current in normal use. Misconception: neutral is not 'safe to touch' because it can be dangerous in a fault.

teach.heading: Why live is dangerous
bullets: The live wire is at 230 V relative to earth.
Touching it completes a path through your body to earth.
This causes a current through you: a shock.
Switches and fuses must be in the live wire.
teach.note: Even if an appliance is switched off, the live wire may be live up to the switch. Ask: why is it dangerous to touch a live wire while standing on the ground, but a bird on a power line is safe? (No potential difference across the bird, no path to the ground). Never touch or investigate sockets at home.

teach.heading: Fuses and earthing
bullets: A fault connects the live wire to the metal case.
Earth wire gives a low-resistance path, so a large current flows.
The fuse melts (blows) and breaks the circuit.
Appliances with plastic cases are double insulated.
teach.note: Walk through the fault scenario slowly with a diagram. Fuse values: 3 A, 5 A, 13 A. Choose a fuse that is slightly above the normal current: e.g. a 920 W iron at 230 V takes 4 A, so use a 5 A fuse. A circuit breaker (RCCB) can also switch off the supply and be reset.

teach.heading: Exam practice: safety explanations
bullets: Use sequence words: first, then, so, therefore.
Name the component and its role.
Mention the large current and the melting fuse.
Take care that live and neutral are not swapped.
teach.note: Model a 4-mark answer: 'If the live wire touches the metal case, the case becomes live. The earth wire provides a low-resistance path to earth. A large current flows, so the fuse melts and disconnects the live wire. This stops the user receiving a shock.' Pupils write their own version in pairs.

practice: State the colours of the live, neutral and earth wires.
A kettle takes 10 A in normal use. Which fuse should be used: 3 A, 5 A or 13 A? Explain.
Why is a switch placed in the live wire rather than in the neutral wire?
independent: Label a diagram of a three-pin plug with wires, fuse and cable grip, and give the function of each.
Explain how an earth wire and a fuse work together to protect a user. (4 marks)
Compare a.c. and d.c., including the source of each. (3 marks)
exit: What are the UK mains potential difference and frequency?
Which wire is the safety wire?
lessons.homework: Design a poster on electrical safety in the home with five rules and a reason for each (no practical work with mains).
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn plug with colour coding to complete. EAL: picture-based key terms. Stretch: calculate the correct fuse for a 2.4 kW heater and justify your choice.

lessons.title: Electrical power and energy transfers
objectives: Use P = I V, P = I²R and E = P t to calculate power and energy
Use E = Q V for energy transferred by charge
Calculate energy use in kilowatt-hours and the cost of running appliances

keywords.def: the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts (W)
the energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour
the amount of energy moved from one store to another, in joules
the fraction of input energy that is usefully transferred

starter: Calculate the p.d. if 240 J of energy is transferred by 20 C of charge.
State the equation linking V, I and R.
Convert 2.3 kW into W.

teach.heading: Electrical power
bullets: Power is the rate of energy transfer, in watts (W).
P = I V (power = current × potential difference).
P = I² R (power = current squared × resistance).
1 W = 1 joule per second.
teach.note: Worked examples: a heater with 3 A at 230 V has P = 3 x 230 = 690 W. A 5 Ω resistor carrying 4 A has P = 4² x 5 = 80 W. Kettle: 2300 W at 230 V means I = P ÷ V = 10 A. Emphasise squaring the current first and writing the unit W.

teach.heading: Energy transferred
bullets: E = P t: energy in joules, power in watts, time in seconds.
E = Q V: energy transferred by charge moving through p.d.
Example: 2000 W for 180 s transfers 360 000 J.
Example: 30 C through 6 V transfers 180 J.
teach.note: Pupils must convert minutes to seconds. Ask: how are P = IV and E = QV linked? Since Q = I t, E = I t V = P t. This shows the links between equations and helps pupils remember them.

teach.heading: Kilowatt-hours and cost
bullets: Energy (kWh) = power (kW) × time (h).
Cost = energy in kWh × cost per kWh.
Example: 2.3 kW kettle for 3 minutes (0.05 h) = 0.115 kWh.
At 28p per kWh that costs about 3.2p.
teach.note: Note that the price per kWh is hypothetical; real prices vary. Compare with joules: 1 kWh = 3 600 000 J, which is why household bills use kWh. Pupils often forget to convert W to kW and minutes to hours.

teach.heading: Energy changes in resistors
bullets: When current flows, electrons collide with ions in the wire.
Electrical energy is transferred to thermal energy (heating effect).
Useful in toasters and kettles; wasteful in cables.
Larger current gives much greater heating (I²).
teach.note: Link back to the wire practical: a wire gets hot. Ask: why do electricity companies transmit at high voltage? (A lower current means less heating, since power loss is I²R.) Mention the National Grid is covered later in the course.

teach.heading: Exam tips for calculations
bullets: Write the equation, then substitute, then calculate.
Check units: W, kW, J, kWh.
Round at the end, quoting appropriate significant figures.
Estimate: does the answer make sense?
teach.note: Provide a checklist and demonstrate a worked six-line solution on the board. Ask pupils to spot a common mistake: using minutes instead of seconds. Remind that Islam encourages avoiding waste (israf), which links to checking appliance energy use.

practice: A 60 W lamp operates for 2 hours. Calculate the energy in kWh.
A toaster draws 4.5 A from a 230 V supply. Calculate its power.
A current of 2 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. Calculate the power.
independent: A 1.8 kW hairdryer is used for 10 minutes each day. Calculate the energy transferred in a week in kWh and the cost at 28p per kWh.
A heater transfers 720 000 J in 5 minutes. Calculate the power in W and kW.
Explain why a 13 A fuse is suitable for a 2 kW kettle but not a 3 A fuse. (3 marks)
exit: Write the equation linking energy, power and time.
How many joules are there in one kilowatt-hour?
lessons.homework: Record the power ratings of five appliances in your home, calculate the energy used in one hour and estimate the daily cost.
lessons.send: SEND: formula sheets with units and worked examples. EAL: pre-teach 'rate' and 'rating'. Stretch: show that doubling the current through a resistor quadruples its power.
